claim: The nucleus accumbens shell (NAc-S) and its projections to the ventral pallidum (VP) are thought to be critical for stimulus-based decisions.
source: The nucleus accumbens shell (NAc-S) and its projections to the ventral pallidum (VP) are thought to be critical for stimulus-based decisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature, as indicated by the context of the abstract.

claim: The NAc-S is predominantly composed of spiny projection neurons (SPNs) that express either the dopamine D1 (D1-SPNs) or the dopamine D2 receptor (D2-SPNs).
source: The NAc-S is predominantly composed of spiny projection neurons (SPNs) that express either the dopamine D1 (D1-SPNs) or the dopamine D2 receptor (D2-SPNs).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the cellular composition of the NAc-S.

claim: Silencing either population of NAc-S SPNs disrupted choice in outcome-specific PIT.
source: Silencing either population of NAc-S SPNs disrupted choice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the optogenetic silencing experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Silencing NAc-S D1-SPNs terminals in the VP disrupted choice in outcome-specific PIT.
source: Silencing NAc-S D1-SPNs terminals in the VP also disrupted choice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the optogenetic silencing experiments targeting D1-SPN terminals in the VP.

claim: Choice was left intact by silencing NAc-S D2-SPNs terminals in the VP.
source: However, choice was left intact by silencing NAc-S D2-SPNs terminals in the VP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the optogenetic silencing experiments targeting D2-SPN terminals in the VP.

claim: These findings are consistent with a recent model proposing that stimulus-based decisions are controlled by an opioid-based memory system residing in the NAc-S.
source: We discuss how these insights are consistent with a recent model proposing that these decisions are controlled by an opioid-based memory system residing in the NAc-S.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings and their alignment with a theoretical model.

claim: Outcome-specific Pavlovian-instrumental transfer (PIT) comprises three stages: Pavlovian conditioning, instrumental conditioning, and a PIT test.
source: This influence is studied in the laboratory using the outcome-specific Pavlovian-instrumental transfer (PIT) task (Trapold and Overmier, 1972; Colwill and Rescorla, 1988; Holmes et al., 2010; Cartoni et al., 2016; Laurent and Balleine, 2021; Leung et al., 2024b), which comprises three stages.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing the PIT task.

claim: In Pavlovian conditioning, two stimuli (S1 and S2) are paired with two distinct and motivationally significant outcomes (O1 and O2).
source: In Pavlovian conditioning, two stimuli (S1 and S2; e.g., sounds or lights) are paired with two distinct and motivationally significant outcomes (O1 and O2; e.g., food outcomes).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: In instrumental conditioning, subjects are trained to perform two actions (A1 and A2), with each earning one of the two outcomes (A1 → O1 and A2 → O2).
source: In instrumental conditioning, subjects are trained to perform two actions (A1 and A2), with each earning one of the two outcomes (i.e., A1 → O1 and A2 → O2).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: During the PIT test, each of the Pavlovian stimuli biases choice toward the action with which it shares an outcome (S1: A1 > A2 and S2: A2 > A1).
source: Typically, each of the Pavlovian stimuli biases choice toward the action with which it shares an outcome: that is, S1: A1 > A2 and S2: A2 > A1.
evidence: This claim describes the typical behavioral outcome observed in PIT tasks.

claim: PIT has been found to rely on interactions between cortical, amygdala, basal ganglia, midbrain, and thalamic structures.
source: At a neural level, PIT has been found to rely on interactions between a number of structures, including cortical (Keistler et al., 2015; Bradfield et al., 2015; Bradfield et al., 2018; Tensaouti et al., 2025; Ostlund and Balleine, 2007; Lichtenberg et al., 2021; Sias et al., 2021; Lichtenberg et al., 2017), amygdala (Corbit and Balleine, 2005; Morse et al., 2020; Sias et al., 2024; Lichtenberg et al., 2017; Shiflett and Balleine, 2010; Derman et al., 2020; Prévost et al., 2012), basal ganglia (Corbit and Balleine, 2011; Corbit et al., 2001; Corbit and Janak, 2010; Morse et al., 2020; Laurent et al., 2012; Bertran-Gonzalez et al., 2013; Laurent et al., 2014; Corbit et al., 2016; Leung et al., 2024a; Leung and Balleine, 2015; Leung and Balleine, 2013; Laurent et al., 2015; Prévost et al., 2012), midbrain (Corbit et al., 2007; Sias et al., 2024; Seitz et al., 2022), and thalamic (Ostlund and Balleine, 2008; Leung et al., 2024a) territories.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The NAc-S does not contribute to learning the stimulus–outcome (S–O) or the action–outcome (A–O) associations formed during the Pavlovian and instrumental stages of the PIT task.
source: Among these, the nucleus accumbens shell (NAc-S) stands out because, unlike the others, it does not itself contribute to learning the stimulus–outcome (S–O) or the action–outcome (A–O) associations formed during the Pavlovian and instrumental stages of the PIT task and appears only to mediate their interaction (Corbit and Balleine, 2011; Corbit et al., 2001; Morse et al., 2020; Laurent et al., 2012; Laurent et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The NAc-S appears only to mediate the interaction between S–O and A–O associations.
source: Among these, the nucleus accumbens shell (NAc-S) stands out because, unlike the others, it does not itself contribute to learning the stimulus–outcome (S–O) or the action–outcome (A–O) associations formed during the Pavlovian and instrumental stages of the PIT task and appears only to mediate their interaction (Corbit and Balleine, 2011; Corbit et al., 2001; Morse et al., 2020; Laurent et al., 2012; Laurent et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The NAc-S acts as a central hub integrating S–O and A–O information at the time of PIT to guide choice between actions in an outcome-selective manner.
source: Therefore, it has been proposed that the NAc-S acts as a central hub integrating S–O and A–O information at the time of PIT to guide choice between actions in an outcome-selective manner (Shiflett and Balleine, 2010; Bertran-Gonzalez and Laurent, 2018; Laurent and Balleine, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PIT is disrupted by manipulations undermining NAc-S function during the PIT test.
source: Accordingly, PIT is disrupted by manipulations undermining NAc-S function during the PIT test (Morse et al., 2020; Corbit et al., 2016; Laurent et al., 2012; Laurent et al., 2014; Laurent et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One population of NAc-S SPNs harbors the dopamine D1 receptors (D1Rs; D1-SPNs), whereas the other population expresses the dopamine D2 receptors (D2Rs; D2-SPNs).
source: The NAc-S is predominantly composed of spiny projection neurons (SPNs), which can be classified into two distinct subpopulations depending on the dopamine receptor they express (Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011). One population harbors the dopamine D1 receptors (D1Rs; D1-SPNs), whereas the other population expresses the dopamine D2 receptors (D2Rs; D2-SPNs).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: PIT is associated with an increase in ERK1/2 phosphorylation in D1-SPNs but not D2-SPNs.
source: To date, only one study has examined whether activity in both populations is recruited during PIT (Laurent et al., 2014), finding that PIT is associated with an increase in ERK1/2 phosphorylation in D1-SPNs but not D2-SPNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Blockade of D1Rs in NAc-S during choice between actions disrupted PIT whereas D2Rs blockade had no effect.
source: Further, blockade of D1Rs in NAc-S during choice between actions disrupted PIT whereas D2Rs blockade had no effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Laurent et al., 2014).

claim: D1Rs are exclusively expressed on NAc-S D1-SPNs.
source: While D1Rs are exclusively expressed on NAc-S D1-SPNs, D2Rs are present on cholinergic interneurons (CINs) and local presynaptic dopamine terminals in addition to D2-SPNs (Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: D2Rs are present on cholinergic interneurons (CINs) and local presynaptic dopamine terminals in addition to D2-SPNs.
source: While D1Rs are exclusively expressed on NAc-S D1-SPNs, D2Rs are present on cholinergic interneurons (CINs) and local presynaptic dopamine terminals in addition to D2-SPNs (Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: ERK1/2 phosphorylation may not capture all transcriptional events that occur in D2-SPNs.
source: Additionally, research shows that ERK1/2 phosphorylation may not capture all transcriptional events that occur in D2-SPNs (Bertran-Gonzalez et al., 2008; Matamales et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pharmacological D2Rs blockade has been found to be quite ineffective at influencing D2-SPNs function.
source: Lastly, pharmacological D2Rs blockade has been found to be quite ineffective at influencing D2-SPNs function (Tozzi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Both NAc-S D1- and D2-SPNs send dense projections to the VP.
source: We focused on the VP for two main reasons: First, both NAc-S D1- and D2-SPNs send dense projections to this region (Lu et al., 1997; Kupchik et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Communication between the NAc-S and VP has previously been found to be critical for outcome-specific PIT.
source: and, second, communication between the NAc-S and VP has previously been found to be critical for outcome-specific PIT (Leung and Balleine, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In D1-Cre and A2a-Cre rats, viral expression was largely restricted to local SPNs in the NAc-S and dorsal striatum: ~95% of eYFP-positive neurons expressed DARPP-32.
source: In both transgenic strains, viral expression was largely restricted to local SPNs in the two targeted regions: ~95% of eYFP-positive neurons expressed DARPP-32 (D32 | eYFP; Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In both D1-Cre and A2a-Cre transgenic strains and targeted regions, ~40% of DARPP-32-positive neurons expressed eYFP.
source: Viral expression was consistent with D1- and D2-SPNs representing two neuronal populations similar in size: in both transgenic strains and targeted regions ~40% of DARPP-32-positive neurons expressed eYFP (eYFP | D32; Figure 1C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1.

claim: DS infusion in D1-Cre rats resulted in eYFP-positive terminals in the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) and the globus pallidus externus (GPe).
source: DS infusion in D1-Cre rats resulted in eYFP-positive terminals (Figure 1B, C) in the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) and the globus pallidus externus (GPe).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: DS infusion in A2a-Cre rats only produced eYFP-positive terminals in the GPe.
source: By contrast, the same infusion in A2a-Cre rats only produced eYFP-positive terminals in the GPe (Figure 1B, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: NAc-S infusion in both D1-Cre and A2a-Cre rats resulted in eYFP-positive terminals in the VP.
source: NAc-S infusion in both D1-Cre and A2a-Cre rats resulted in eYFP-positive terminals in the VP (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: eYFP-positive terminals in the lateral hypothalamus were only observed in D1-Cre rats following NAc-S infusion.
source: By contrast, eYFP-positive terminals in the lateral hypothalamus (Figure 1E, F) were only observed in D1-Cre rats.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1.

claim: LED light illumination (625 nm, continuous) of NAc-S D1-SPNs transfected with the eYFP virus had no effect on action potential firing.
source: LED light illumination (625 nm, continuous) of either NAc-S D1-SPNs (Figure 2A) or NAc-S D2-SPNs (Figure 2B) transfected with the eYFP virus had no effect on action potential firing (Baseline vs. LED ON; D1-Cre: p = 1, 5 cells; A2A-Cre: p = 0.35, 8 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2.

claim: LED light illumination (625 nm, continuous) of NAc-S D2-SPNs transfected with the eYFP virus had no effect on action potential firing.
source: LED light illumination (625 nm, continuous) of either NAc-S D1-SPNs (Figure 2A) or NAc-S D2-SPNs (Figure 2B) transfected with the eYFP virus had no effect on action potential firing (Baseline vs. LED ON; D1-Cre: p = 1, 5 cells; A2A-Cre: p = 0.35, 8 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2.

claim: LED light illumination onto NAc-S D1-SPNs transfected with eNpHR3.0 suppressed action potential firing.
source: By contrast, the same illumination onto NAc-S D1- (Figure 2A) or D2-SPNs (Figure 2B) transfected with eNpHR3.0 suppressed action potential firing (D1-Cre: F(1,6) = 16.82; η2 = 0.74, p < 0.001, 7 cells; A2A-Cre: F(1,5) = 135.00; η2 = 0.96, p < 0.001, 6 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2.

claim: LED light illumination onto NAc-S D2-SPNs transfected with eNpHR3.0 suppressed action potential firing.
source: By contrast, the same illumination onto NAc-S D1- (Figure 2A) or D2-SPNs (Figure 2B) transfected with eNpHR3.0 suppressed action potential firing (D1-Cre: F(1,6) = 16.82; η2 = 0.74, p < 0.001, 7 cells; A2A-Cre: F(1,5) = 135.00; η2 = 0.96, p < 0.001, 6 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There was no difference in firing prior to or following LED light illumination in eNpHR3.0-transfected neurons, indicating that the optical manipulation did not alter D1- or D2-SPNs physiology.
source: Importantly, there was no difference in firing prior to or following LED light illumination, indicating that the optical manipulation did not alter D1- or D2-SPNs physiology.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the electrophysiological data.

claim: Rats in the eYFP group displayed intact outcome-specific PIT whether the LED light was OFF or ON.
source: Follow-up analyses revealed that rats in the eYFP group displayed intact outcome-specific PIT whether the LED light was OFF (F(1,9) = 6.14; η2 = 0.67; p < 0.05) or ON (F(1,9) = 39.46; η2 = 0.81; p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the PIT test shown in Figure 3.

claim: Rats in the eNpHR3.0 group (D1-Cre) displayed outcome-specific PIT when the light was OFF but not when it was ON.
source: By contrast, rats in the eNpHR3.0 group displayed outcome-specific PIT when the light was OFF (F(1,9) = 12.38; η2 = 0.58; p < 0.01) but not when it was ON (p = 0.67).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the PIT test shown in Figure 3.

claim: Activity in NAc-S D1-SPNs is necessary for the outcome-specific influence exerted by predictive stimuli on choice between actions.
source: Together, these results indicate that activity in NAc-S D1-SPNs is necessary for the outcome-specific influence exerted by predictive stimuli on choice between actions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that silencing D1-SPNs disrupts PIT.

claim: Silencing NAc-S D1-SPNs had no effect on value-based choice.
source: Importantly, the impairment produced by silencing NAc-S D1-SPNs was restricted to the influence of predictive stimuli on choice between actions. In the same rats, we found that this silencing had no effect on value-based choice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and Appendix 2) using an outcome devaluation procedure: all rats performed the action that previously earned a valuable outcome more than the action that earned a devalued outcome.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the choice test shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: NAc-S lesion or inactivation spares value-based choice.
source: This agrees with studies reporting that NAc-S lesion or inactivation spares value-based choice (Corbit and Balleine, 2011; Corbit et al., 2001; Morse et al., 2020; Laurent et al., 2012; Laurent et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Control eYFP rats (A2a-Cre) expressed outcome-specific PIT whether the LED light was OFF or ON.
source: Follow-up analyses revealed that control eYFP rats expressed outcome-specific PIT whether the LED light was OFF (F(1,7) = 16.25; η2 = 0.70; p < 0.01) or ON (F(1,7) = 20.58; η2 = 0.75; p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the PIT test shown in Figure 4.

claim: Rats in the eNpHR3.0 group (A2a-Cre) displayed outcome-specific PIT when the light was OFF but not ON.
source: By contrast, rats in the eNpHR3.0 group displayed outcome-specific PIT when the light was OFF (F(1,5) = 6.94; η2 = 0.58; p < 0.05) but not ON (p = 0.34).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the PIT test shown in Figure 4.

claim: Activity in NAc-S D2-SPNs is necessary for the outcome-specific influence exerted by predictive stimuli on choice between actions.
source: Thus, these results show for the first time that activity in NAc-S D2-SPNs is necessary for the outcome-specific influence exerted by predictive stimuli on choice between actions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that silencing D2-SPNs disrupts PIT.

claim: Silencing NAc-S D2-SPNs had no effect on value-based choice.
source: Importantly, we also found that the impairment produced by silencing NAc-S D2-SPNs was restricted to the influence of predictive stimuli on choice between actions. In the same rats, this silencing had no effect on value-based choice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the choice test shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: A D2Rs antagonist could be expected to enhance D2-SPN activity, since D2Rs are Gi coupled and so their activation should reduce adenylyl cyclase activity.
source: For instance, a D2Rs antagonist could be expected to enhance D2-SPN activity, since D2Rs are Gi coupled and so their activation should reduce adenylyl cyclase activity.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about D2 receptor signaling.

claim: Control eYFP rats (D1-Cre, VP terminals) expressed outcome-specific PIT whether the LED light was OFF or ON.
source: Follow-up analyses revealed that control eYFP rats expressed outcome-specific PIT whether the LED light was OFF (F(1,7) = 26.63; η2 = 0.79; p < 0.001) or ON (F(1,7) = 12.31; η2 = 0.64; p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the PIT test shown in Figure 5.

claim: Rats in the eNpHR3.0 group (D1-Cre, VP terminals) displayed outcome-specific PIT when the light was OFF but not ON.
source: By contrast, rats in the eNpHR3.0 group displayed outcome-specific PIT when the light was OFF (F(1,11) = 26.53; η2 = 0.71; p < 0.001) but not ON (p = 0.48).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the PIT test shown in Figure 5.

claim: NAc-S D1-SPNs mediate outcome-specific PIT via their projections to the VP.
source: Thus, these results show for the first time that NAc-S D1-SPNs mediate outcome-specific PIT via their projections to the VP.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that silencing D1-SPN terminals in the VP disrupts PIT.

claim: Silencing NAc-S D1-SPNs terminals in the VP had no effect on value-based choice.
source: Importantly, we also found that the impairment produced by silencing NAc-S D1-SPNs terminals in the VP was restricted to the influence of predictive stimuli on choice between actions. In the same rats, this silencing had no effect on value-based choice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the choice test shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Silencing NAc-S D2-SPNs projections to the VP had no effect on outcome-specific PIT.
source: Silencing NAc-S D2-SPNs projections to the VP had no effect on outcome-specific PIT.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the PIT test shown in Figure 6.

claim: NAc-S D2-SPNs do not appear to mediate outcome-specific PIT via their projections to the VP.
source: Thus, NAc-S D2-SPNs do not appear to mediate outcome-specific PIT via their projections to the VP.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that silencing D2-SPN terminals in the VP does not disrupt PIT.

claim: Silencing NAc-S D2-SPNs terminals in the VP had no effect on value-based choice.
source: Likewise, we found no evidence that these projections influence value-based choice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the choice test shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Both NAc-S D1- and D2-SPN populations contribute to PIT expression.
source: Additionally, they showed that this choice is also abolished by silencing NAc-S D2-SPNs, providing the first evidence that both SPN populations contribute to PIT expression.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that silencing either D1- or D2-SPNs disrupts PIT.

claim: Outcome-specific choice is likely to involve downstream regulation of VP function by NAc-S D1-SPNs but not NAc-S D2-SPNs.
source: Finally, the last two experiments revealed for the first time that outcome-specific choice is likely to involve downstream regulation of VP function by NAc-S D1-SPNs but not NAc-S D2-SPNs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing differential effects of silencing D1- vs D2-SPN terminals in the VP.

claim: The effect of NAc-S D1-SPNs silencing was specific to the assessment of choice between actions in the presence of predictive stimuli.
source: Importantly, the effect of NAc-S D1-SPNs silencing was specific to the assessment of choice between actions in the presence of predictive stimuli.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing selective effects on PIT but not other behaviors.

claim: The ability of stimuli to elicit approach behaviors toward the magazine remained intact despite NAc-S D1-SPNs silencing.
source: For instance, the ability of stimuli to elicit approach behaviors toward the magazine remained intact despite NAc-S D1-SPNs silencing, indicating that the silencing effect was not mediated by modulating potential competition between Pavlovian and instrumental responses (Lovibond, 1981; Holmes et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing no effect on magazine entries.

claim: NAc-S D1-SPNs silencing preserved the capacity to select between actions based on the value of their respective outcomes.
source: Furthermore, NAc-S D1-SPNs silencing preserved the capacity to select between actions based on the value of their respective outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the outcome devaluation test.

claim: The NAc-S does not contribute to learning and retrieving the S–O and A–O associations produced by Pavlovian and instrumental conditioning.
source: This selectivity in the impairment produced by NAc-S D1-SPNs is consistent with previous findings demonstrating that the NAc-S does not contribute to learning and retrieving the S–O and A–O associations produced by Pavlovian and instrumental conditioning (Corbit and Balleine, 2011; Corbit et al., 2001; Morse et al., 2020; Laurent et al., 2012; Laurent et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A2a receptors are predominantly expressed on striatal D2-SPNs.
source: A2a receptors are predominantly expressed on striatal D2-SPNs (Schiffmann et al., 2007), thereby enabling selective targeting of these SPNs in the A2a-Cre line.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The VP is often described as the major efferent of the nucleus accumbens.
source: Consistent with the literature (Lu et al., 1997; Kupchik et al., 2015), we found that both NAc-S D1- and D2-SPNs send dense projections to the VP, which is often described as the major efferent of the nucleus accumbens (Heimer et al., 1991; Zahm and Heimer, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The VP has been shown to play a crucial role in outcome-specific choice.
source: Importantly, the VP has been shown to play a crucial role in outcome-specific choice (Leung and Balleine, 2013; Leung and Balleine, 2015; Leung et al., 2024a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VP neurons exhibit enhanced cFos activation following an outcome-specific PIT test, and their levels of activation correlate with PIT performance.
source: VP neurons exhibit enhanced cFos activation following an outcome-specific PIT test, and their levels of activation correlate with PIT performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (implied from context).

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of the VP eliminates outcome-specific choice.
source: Moreover, pharmacological inactivation of the VP eliminates outcome-specific choice, and the same elimination is observed when the NAc-S is disconnected from the VP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (implied from context).

claim: The same elimination of outcome-specific choice is observed when the NAc-S is disconnected from the VP.
source: Moreover, pharmacological inactivation of the VP eliminates outcome-specific choice, and the same elimination is observed when the NAc-S is disconnected from the VP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (implied from context).

claim: NAc-S D2-SPNs appear to exclusively project to the VP.
source: Since NAc-S D2-SPNs appear to exclusively project to the VP (Humphries and Prescott, 2010; Kupchik et al., 2015), our findings suggest that these SPNs mediate outcome-specific PIT by locally regulating NAc-S function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NAc-S D2-SPNs mediate outcome-specific PIT by locally regulating NAc-S function.
source: Since NAc-S D2-SPNs appear to exclusively project to the VP (Humphries and Prescott, 2010; Kupchik et al., 2015), our findings suggest that these SPNs mediate outcome-specific PIT by locally regulating NAc-S function.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and prior literature.

claim: It remains to be determined whether NAc-S D1-SPNs also coordinate outcome-specific PIT via their projections to the lateral hypothalamus and/or the ventral tegmental area (VTA), in addition to the VP.
source: By contrast, it remains to be determined whether NAc-S D1-SPNs also coordinate outcome-specific PIT via their projections to the lateral hypothalamus (O'Connor et al., 2015) and/or the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Humphries and Prescott, 2010), in addition to the VP.
evidence: This claim is speculative about future research directions.

claim: Outcome-specific choice in PIT relies on an opioid-based memory residing in the NAc-S.
source: The present findings are consistent with a recent model proposing that outcome-specific choice in PIT relies on an opioid-based memory residing in the NAc-S (for full description and illustration of the model see Leung et al., 2024b; Laurent and Balleine, 2021; Morse et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing a theoretical model.

claim: As the basolateral amygdala encodes and stores outcome-specific S–O associations across Pavlovian conditioning, it also drives the formation of the NAc-S memory, which involves the durable accumulation of delta-opioid receptors (DOPRs) on the somatic membrane of local CINs.
source: In this model, as the basolateral amygdala encodes and stores outcome-specific S–O associations across Pavlovian conditioning, it also drives the formation of the NAc-S memory, which involves the durable accumulation of delta-opioid receptors (DOPRs) on the somatic membrane of local CINs (Bertran-Gonzalez et al., 2013; Morse et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing a theoretical model.

claim: The NAc-S memory is not necessary for Pavlovian conditioning per se, but its expression is later required to enable the predictive stimuli to guide outcome-specific choice during the PIT test.
source: Although this memory is not necessary for Pavlovian conditioning per se, its expression is later required to enable the predictive stimuli to guide outcome-specific choice during the PIT test (Morse et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Memory expression in the NAc-S is controlled by fluctuations in glutamatergic release from cortical inputs and dopamine release from projections originating from the VTA.
source: The model specifically proposes that memory expression is controlled by fluctuations in glutamatergic release from cortical inputs and dopamine release from projections originating from the VTA, as this brain region has been found to be important for outcome-specific PIT (Corbit et al., 2007; Sias et al., 2024; Seitz et al., 2022; Leung and Balleine, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing a theoretical model.

claim: One consequence of memory expression is to activate NAc-S D2-SPNs and enkephalin discharge by these neurons.
source: One consequence is to activate NAc-S D2-SPNs and enkephalin discharge by these neurons.
evidence: This claim is part of a theoretical model described in the manuscript.

claim: Enkephalin binds onto DOPRs that had accumulated on local CINs and dampens acetylcholine secretion from the interneurons.
source: Enkephalin then binds onto DOPRs that had accumulated on local CINs and dampens acetylcholine secretion from the interneurons.
evidence: This claim is part of a theoretical model described in the manuscript.
